newsitem.title: CHINA: Victims' kin want probe into China '89 crackdown.
newsitem.headline: Victims' kin want probe into China '89 crackdown.

text.p: Bereaved relatives of people killed in China's 1989 army crackdown on a democracy movement have called for an official inquiry into the deaths, one of the relatives said on Wednesday.
Forty-two relatives of victims of the crackdown in Beijing on June 4, 1989, sent a petition to the standing committee of the National People's Congress, or parliament, on May 15.
The petition also called for a "direct, sincere diaologue" with the parliament which has ignored similar petitions in the past two years.

"We believe the government's actions in the bloody tragedy of eight years ago were not just improperly handled," said Ding Zilin, one of the signatories. Ding's 17-year-old son was killed in the crackdown.
"On the contrary, the government committed a crime against the people," she told Reuters.
Ding, a retired associate professor of philosophy at People's University, published a book containing a partial list of about 150 victims.

The relatives made the petition just weeks before the eighth anniversary of the crackdown, ordered by paramount leader Deng Xiaoping. Army tanks and bullets left hundreds dead in the streets of Beijing.
Hundreds more were jailed or fled abroad in the following months.
Deng died in February aged 92.

In the petition, the group called on parliament to set up an independent board to investigate the 1989 events and pass laws allowing relatives of victims to seek compensation from the government, Ding said.
Ding said parliament had not yet responded to the petition, and the group had sent dozens of letters to leading lawmakers urging them to take action.
"We feel the goals of these demands have been set quite high and their realisation is far off, but we have patience," said Ding.
"What does time matter to us?" Ding asked. "Our loved ones will never come back."
Parliamentary officials were not immediately available for comment.
China has defended the crackdown, saying the protests and rallies that swept the country were crimes of counter-revolution, or subversion.
"A new assessment of the June 4 incident must be made," said the petition, a copy of which was seen by Reuters.

Ding and the other petitioners had also called on Beijing to explain remarks made by Chinese Defence Minister Chi Haotian to the U.S. Congress last December asserting that no one was killed in Beijing's Tiananmen Square, centre of the protests.
"Does Chi's speech in fact represent his personal views or those of the government?" the petition asked.

Ding said she was often watched and followed by plainclothes police but had detected no increased surveillance in the run-up to the emotive June 4 anniversary. She added such scrutiny was unnecessary.
"We're not out to make any trouble, we are just mailing some letters," she said.
